intro: Roosendaal's registered trees stand in five public places across town. De Kring square holds a pair of planes: a rare Oriental plane from around 1850, the wilder parent of the London plane, with a London plane from the 1900s in front of it. Emile van Loonpark holds a horse chestnut that flowers every May. On Burgerhoutsestraat a catalpa, a London plane and a Cedar of Lebanon share the garden of Villa Van Gilse. The Paterstuin behind the Onze Lieve Vrouwekerk holds a Himalayan cedar, and in the old Bachlaan cemetery a double-flowered horse chestnut stands alone among the graves.
meta_description: Thirteen registered trees in Roosendaal and Nispen: planes at De Kring, two cedars, a cemetery chestnut, a copper beech and two royal limes.
question_meta: Roosendaal's oldest tree is an Oriental plane at De Kring, banded to around 1850 and roughly 180 years old. Its story and twelve more.
question_answer: The oldest tree in Roosendaal is the Oriental Plane of De Kring, which the national tree register bands to a planting around 1850, roughly 180 years old. It stands on De Kring square, a rare tree in a country whose squares are planted with London planes.
question_context: Ages here come from the Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen, which records a planting decade rather than a year, so every figure on this page is a band. Nine of the thirteen trees stand in five spots in town; four more stand in the village of Nispen, 6 km south. De Kring square holds the Oriental plane with a London plane from the 1900s 13 metres in front. Emile van Loonpark holds a horse chestnut behind the pond, from around 1870. The garden of Villa Van Gilse on Burgerhoutsestraat holds a catalpa, a London plane and a Cedar of Lebanon. The Paterstuin behind the Onze Lieve Vrouwekerk holds a Himalayan cedar and a row of horse chestnuts. The Algemene Begraafplaats on Bachlaan holds a double-flowered horse chestnut from the 1870s. Nispen holds a copper beech of fused stems at its parish cemetery gate, limes planted in 1909 and 1938 for the births of Princesses Juliana and Beatrix, and a roadside oak from the 1920s. All thirteen are free to see; the Bachlaan cemetery is open daily from 8.00 to 16.30 and the Paterstuin in daylight. Where a pin is marked approximate, we know the site and not the exact trunk.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Roosendaal?
faq.a: The Oriental Plane of De Kring, banded by the national tree register to a planting around 1850, roughly 180 years old. It stands on De Kring square, in the middle of town.

faq.q: What happened to the old lime in Emile van Loonpark?
faq.a: The national register records it as declared dead in 1998. The park's horse chestnut, behind the pond, is still there.

faq.q: Why does an Oriental plane at De Kring stand out?
faq.a: Most planes planted on Dutch squares are London planes, a hybrid bred from the Oriental species and an American one. This is the wilder-growing parent itself, native to southeast Europe and western Asia, planted here around 1850.

faq.q: Are these trees free to visit?
faq.a: Yes. Every tree on this list stands on a public square, park, garden, street or cemetery with nothing to pay. The cemetery on Bachlaan is open daily from 8.00 to 16.30 and the Paterstuin garden in daylight, closing at dusk; the others can be seen at any time.

trees.name: The Oriental Plane of De Kring
trees.age_estimate: roughly 180 years, from a registered planting date around 1850
trees.story:
This Oriental plane stands by De Kring, a public square in Roosendaal, banded by the national register to a planting around 1850, roughly 180 years old. A horse chestnut of about the same age once shared the square with it; the register records that tree felled in 2014 and a young one planted in its place, which leaves the plane as the oldest trunk on De Kring. A London plane from around 1900 to 1910 stands about 13 metres east, in front of it.

Oriental plane is the older, wilder-growing parent of the hybrid London plane that lines so many European streets, native to southeast Europe and western Asia, and it is planted less often in the Netherlands than its more tolerant offspring. Left to grow on an open square rather than pruned to a street profile, an Oriental plane develops the same flaking, camouflage-patterned bark as its hybrid relative but with a more irregular, spreading crown, often leaning and forking low rather than rising in a single clean trunk.

The register records the species and the decade but nothing of who planted it or why, which is typical for a tree whose interest is simply having survived on the same square for nearly two centuries while whatever stood around it changed. If you know more of De Kring's own history, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the back one of the two old planes in this corner of De Kring, 4.5 metres round. The younger London plane stands about 13 metres east, in front of it.

trees.name: The Catalpa of Burgerhoutsestraat
trees.age_estimate: roughly 130 years, from a registered planting date around 1900
trees.story:
This catalpa stands southwest of a building on Burgerhoutsestraat, banded by the national register to a planting around 1900, roughly 130 years old. A London plane the register also lists grows at the front of the same building, so the property carries two registered trees framing it from different sides, one native to the eastern United States and one a hybrid bred in seventeenth century Europe.

Southern catalpa is grown for its broad, heart-shaped leaves and, through midsummer, loose clusters of white flowers marked with purple and yellow spots inside each throat, followed by long, bean-like seed pods that can hang on the bare branches well into winter, giving the species its other common name, Indian bean tree, despite having no connection to India.

A catalpa at 130 years is well into a mature specimen's proportions, wide-crowned and often leaning or multi-stemmed if it was ever cut back hard when young. The register records nothing of who planted it or why, only the species and the decade. If you know more about this tree or the building it stands beside, tell us.

best_time.label: July, when the orchid-like flowers open in loose clusters across the crown

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the broad heart-shaped leaves and the long bean-like pods that hang on into winter. It stands southwest of the building at Burgerhoutsestraat 12; the registered tree at the front is a plane.

trees.name: The Horse Chestnut of the Pond
trees.age_estimate: roughly 160 years, from a registered planting date around 1870

location.address: Roosendaal, Emile van Loonpark, achter vijver

trees.story:
This horse chestnut stands behind the pond in Emile van Loonpark, banded by the national register to a planting around 1870, roughly 160 years old. The park once held an older tree still, a Dutch lime the register bands to somewhere between 1750 and 1800, but the register records that lime as declared dead in 1998, so this chestnut is the park's registered veteran now.

A horse chestnut planted beside water has usually had reliable growing conditions its whole life, and at 160 years this one should show the full domed crown and heavy branch structure the species develops when left largely alone. Every May it produces the upright white flower spikes chestnuts are planted for across Europe, and reflected in the pond behind it, the display reads differently than a chestnut standing on hard pavement elsewhere in this list.

The register gives no further history for this tree, only species and decade. Emile van Loonpark is public and open daily, and this chestnut is the reason to walk to the far side of the pond rather than stopping at the park's edge. If you know more about it, tell us.

best_time.label: May, when the white flower spikes cover the crown and reflect in the pond

trees.verify_notes: 2026-09-08: the story claimed the park's lime was declared dead in 1998 and that this chestnut was therefore the park's surviving veteran. Both halves are wrong. The Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen still carries nr 1680922, Hollandse linde, Emile van Loonpark, band 1750-1800, and it is not among the register's dead entries. We publish that lime ourselves as roo_010, so the page contradicted its own neighbour. Sentence replaced with what the register says. 2026-10-12: reversed. The live LRMB layer now carries nr 1680922 as status 5, Dood/geveld, with 'In 1998 al dood verklaard' and an inspector's 'onvindbaar' on 2018-08-29; roo_010 was retired the same day and the story says the lime is gone.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the white flower candles in May, reflected in the water behind it. It stands on the far side of the pond in Emile van Loonpark, so keep walking rather than stopping at the park's edge.

trees.name: The Plane of Burgerhoutsestraat
trees.age_estimate: roughly 160 years, from a registered planting date around 1870

location.address: Roosendaal, Burgerhoutsestraat 12, aan de voorzijde van het gebouw

trees.story:
This London plane stands at the front of the same Burgerhoutsestraat building whose southwest corner holds a registered catalpa, banded by the national register to a planting around 1870, roughly 160 years old and a generation younger than its catalpa neighbour on the other side of the same property.

London plane is the hybrid that resulted from crossing an American and an Oriental species in seventeenth century Europe, and it turned out to tolerate compacted soil, air pollution and hard pruning better than almost any other large tree available, which is why it became the default choice for European streets and squares from the eighteenth century onward. Its bark flakes away in patches rather than splitting, leaving a mottled grey, green and cream pattern across the trunk that keeps changing as old plates drop and new bark shows through underneath.

At the front of a building rather than tucked behind it, this plane has likely had more pruning against passing traffic than its catalpa neighbour, which a plane tolerates without much complaint. The register records only species and decade. If you know the building's own history, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the bark, flaking away in patches to leave a mottled grey, green and cream trunk. It stands at the front of the building at Burgerhoutsestraat 12; the catalpa is round at the southwest corner.

trees.name: The London Plane of De Kring
trees.age_estimate: roughly 120 years, from a registered planting decade
trees.access: Free. Public square (plein) owned by the municipality, register: visitable ja, visible ja, openbaar ja. No hours; open at all times.
trees.transport: Roosendaal station is about 0.8 km north, roughly a 10 minute walk via Stationsstraat and Kerkstraat.
trees.story:
The national tree register describes this London plane by the tree behind it. About 13 metres west stands the Oriental plane of De Kring, one of the two species the London plane was bred from, so this corner of the square puts a hybrid and its parent side by side.

This is the front tree and the younger of the pair, banded by the register to a planting between 1900 and 1910, which makes it roughly 116 to 126 years old. The register gives it 25 metres of height to the Oriental plane's 22, and a trunk 3.6 metres round at chest height.

The pair have not had an easy century. In 2002 the Bomenstichting, the Dutch tree foundation, studied the ground beneath them and advised keeping both planes. Building went ahead anyway, inside the spread of their crowns and their roots. When the register last checked, in July 2023, it was mostly the Oriental plane behind whose crown had gone thin, with dead tips on its branches. This one is not the tree it describes as declining.

A horse chestnut once made this a trio. The register records it felled in 2014 and a young tree planted in its place, so that young tree is not part of the old group.

The register is the only source for this tree, and July 2023 is the last time it was recorded standing. If you have walked past it since, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the front one of the two old planes in this corner of De Kring, in its own round tree pit. The rarer Oriental plane stands about 13 metres west, behind it.

trees.name: The Baumann's Horse Chestnut of the Algemene Begraafplaats
trees.age_estimate: roughly 150 years, from a registered planting decade

location.address: Roosendaal, Bachlaan 1, Algemene Begraafplaats (closed municipal cemetery)

verified_sources: https://lokaleregelgeving.overheid.nl/CVDR10613 (Verordening op het beheer en het gebruik van de gesloten gemeentelijke begraafplaatsen, art. 2 para 1: open to everyone daily 8.00 to 16.30)
trees.access: Free. Municipal closed cemetery, open to everyone daily 8.00 to 16.30 (municipal cemetery regulation, art. 2; Oorlogsgraf.nl gives the same hours and says dogs are not allowed). Register: visitable ja, owner gemeente.
trees.transport: About 1.5 km east of Roosendaal station, roughly a 20 minute walk via Bredaseweg; parking for about 10 cars in front of the cemetery.
trees.story:
Every May this horse chestnut covers itself in white flowers, and every autumn it drops not a single conker. It is 'Baumannii', the double-flowered clone of the ordinary horse chestnut, and its flowers set no fruit.

The national tree register bands its planting to the 1870s, roughly 146 to 156 years ago. Sources disagree on when the Algemene Begraafplaats itself opened, somewhere between about 1880 and 1894, so the tree may be as old as the cemetery or older. Nobody has recorded how it came to stand here.

It has seen the cemetery's whole working life. Roosendaal buried its dead here until 1978, when the ground closed to new burials, and the chestnut stayed on among the grave rows, alone, 18 metres tall and 3.64 metres round at chest height.

Age has left its mark. The register notes a split in the main fork with small cracks beneath it, and in December 1999 the crown was thinned and anchored. It was inspected again in May 2025 and is still listed as monumental.

That register is the only record of this tree we have found; if you know its history, tell us. The cemetery is open daily from 8.00 to 16.30, and dogs are not allowed.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the lone big horse chestnut among the grave rows, 3.64 metres round, with no other crown within about 8 metres. In May its flowers are double, and in autumn it bears no conkers.

best_time.label: May, when double white flower candles cover the crown

trees.name: The Copper Beech of Nispen Cemetery
trees.age_estimate: roughly 175 years, from a registered planting decade

location.address: Nispen, Heijbeeksestraat, at the entrance of the parish cemetery

trees.access: Free. Stands at the cemetery entrance beside the public Heijbeeksestraat and is visible from the street. Register: visitable ja, visible ja, openbaar ja, owner a religious body (parish). No cemetery hours found.
trees.transport: Nispen is about 6 km south of Roosendaal station (about 20 minutes by bike or car); a bus connection was not confirmed, check 9292 for the Nispen stop. 650 m from the Julianalinde (roo_013).
trees.story:
The thickest beech in Roosendaal's part of the national tree register is really three trunks grown into one. At chest height the copper beech at the gate of Nispen's parish cemetery measures 4.9 metres round, more than any other beech the register lists for Roosendaal. Look lower and the trick shows: 40 centimetres above the ground it is three stems, fused higher up into one flat, oval column. The register says so itself, so read the 490 as the girth of a fused mass rather than of a single trunk.

The height needs no footnote. It stands 26 metres tall, a purple crown over the corner where the cemetery entrance meets Heijbeeksestraat.

The Bomenstichting's Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen puts its planting in the decade 1840 to 1850, which makes it roughly 175 years old. That register is the only source behind this entry, but it is a recent one: an inspector looked at the tree in September 2023 and kept it on the list as monumental. The ground belongs to the parish of the Maria Hemelvaartkerk, whose church stands in front of the cemetery.

You can see it from the street without going in. Nispen lies about six kilometres south of Roosendaal, close to the Belgian border, and the lime the village planted in 1909 for the birth of Princess Juliana stands 650 metres away.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its purple-leaved crown, 26 metres tall, on a trunk that splits into three stems just above the ground. It stands at the cemetery entrance on the corner with Heijbeeksestraat, behind the Maria Hemelvaartkerk.

best_time.label: late October into November, when the purple leaves turn copper before they fall

trees.name: The Julianalinde of Nispen

location.address: Nispen, corner of Dorpsstraat and De Lind

verified_sources: https://www.heemkundenispen.nl/oranjebomen_julianalinde.htm (Heemkundekring de Heerlijckheijd Nispen: Julianalinde, planting 24 May 1909, adopted 1993)
trees.access: Free. Municipal green triangle (plantsoen) at a village street corner, public at all times. Register: visitable ja, visible ja, owner gemeente.
trees.transport: Nispen is about 6 km south of Roosendaal station (about 20 minutes by bike or car); a bus connection was not confirmed, check 9292 for the Nispen stop. 650 m from the cemetery beech (roo_012).
trees.story:
Somewhere under this lime's roots lies a bottle with a letter in it. In May 1909 Nispen's Oranje-Comité planted the tree to mark the birth of Princess Juliana on 30 April, and a charter signed by mayor Coenen and the committee members was sealed in the bottle and buried at its foot. The village schoolchildren took part. The two sources disagree by a day on the planting, the 24th or the 25th of May, so May 1909 is as close as anyone can honestly put it.

The princess became queen in 1948. The tree stayed on its grass triangle where Dorpsstraat meets De Lind, and the village kept coming back to it. In 1993 the local history society, Heemkundekring de Heerlijckheijd Nispen, formally adopted the Julianalinde, and its sign was unveiled by Catharina Verhoeven, who had been one of the children at the planting 84 years earlier. For the hundredth year, in 2009, the society held an exhibition at the tree and the Oranje-Comité gave it an orange nest box.

Today it is 2.82 metres round and 18 metres tall, a common lime by the national register's identification. The register last checked it in April 2024 and found it in reasonable condition, with one complaint: the paving has closed in around it, and the inspector advised giving it a better place to grow.

It is free to visit at any hour, 650 metres from the copper beech at the cemetery gate.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the lone lime on the grass triangle where Dorpsstraat meets De Lind, its trunk 2.82 metres round. It stands in the middle of Nispen, 650 metres from the copper beech at the cemetery.

best_time.label: late June into July, when the cream flowers open and the corner hums with bees

trees.name: The Oak of Nispen
trees.age_estimate: roughly 100 years, from a registered planting decade

location.address: Nispen, Essenseweg 35, roadside at the edge of a maize field

trees.access: Free. Stands in the road verge beside the public Essenseweg at the edge of a field, owner gemeente. Register: visitable ja, visible ja, openbaar ja. Open at all times; view from the road.
trees.transport: Nispen is about 6 km south of Roosendaal station (about 20 minutes by bike or car); a bus connection was not confirmed, check 9292 for the Nispen stop. About 320 m from the cemetery copper beech (roo_012).
trees.story:
This oak stands in three places at once: partly in the field, partly in the road verge and partly under the paving of Essenseweg. The national tree register records all three, and at its last visit, in March 2024, the inspector noted that the road did not seem to bother the base of the trunk.

The Bomenstichting's Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen bands its planting to the 1920s, which makes it roughly 96 to 106 years old. It is 3.05 metres round at chest height and 18 metres tall, and it stands on its own at the edge of the farmland.

The register's file puts it in a larger landscape. Nispen, it says, is the oldest settlement for a long way around, and land consolidation, the Dutch ruilverkaveling, redrew the fields here drastically. The file does not say when, or what this tree saw of it. What it does record is a rough patch in August 2003: storm damage and dead wood in the crown, with advice to cut back the suckers and check the base of the trunk for damage. In 2024 the inspector found it in good condition, and the file describes a healthy tree with a fine crown.

That register is the only source we have for this oak, so nobody has written down who planted it or why. If you know, tell us.

It is free to see from the road at any hour, about 320 metres from the copper beech at Nispen's parish cemetery.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the lone oak at the edge of the field on Essenseweg, its trunk 3.05 metres round and partly in the road paving. It stands about 320 metres from the copper beech at the parish cemetery.

trees.name: The Beatrixlinde of Nispen

location.address: Nispen, corner of Bergsebaan and Klokbergsestraat

verified_sources: https://www.heemkundenispen.nl/oranjebomen_beatrixlinde.htm (Heemkundekring de Heerlijckheijd Nispen: Beatrixlinde, memorial tree planted 1 February 1938, adopted 30 April 1993, stands at the corner of Bergsebaan and Klokbergsestraat)
trees.access: Free. Stands on the open gravel verge at a public village street corner (Bergsebaan/Klokbergsestraat), owner gemeente. Register: visitable ja, visible ja, openbaar ja. Open at all times.
trees.transport: Nispen is about 6 km south of Roosendaal station (about 20 minutes by bike or car); a bus connection was not confirmed, check 9292 for the Nispen stop. About 670 m from the cemetery copper beech (roo_012) and 560 m from the Julianalinde (roo_013).
trees.story:
Nispen planted this lime the day after Princess Beatrix was born. She arrived on 31 January 1938, and on 1 February, according to the village's local history society, Nispen went to mass, walked in procession through the streets and put a memorial tree in the ground. Then came a football match, folk games and, after dark, a torchlight procession.

The national tree register agrees on the year, listing it as a Beatrix tree from 1938, and identifies it as an American lime of the cultivar 'Nova', a different species from the common lime Nispen planted for Juliana in 1909. Today it is 2.83 metres round at chest height and 19 metres tall, standing alone on open gravel at the corner of Bergsebaan and Klokbergsestraat. It carries an old frost crack on its south side. The register last checked it in September 2023 and kept it on the list as monumental.

The baby became queen in 1980. On 30 April 1993, Queen's Day, the Heemkundekring de Heerlijckheijd Nispen adopted the tree, and by its own account has decorated it with a few plants every Queen's Day since.

Not every account agrees on which royal tree stands where. A regional history article puts a Juliana tree at this same corner and calls the date of the Beatrix planting unknown. The register and the history society both place the Beatrix lime here, and the question has not been settled.

It is free to visit at any hour, 560 metres from the Julianalinde.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the lone lime on the open gravel at the corner of Bergsebaan and Klokbergsestraat, 2.83 metres round with an old frost crack on its south side. It stands 560 metres from the Julianalinde.

trees.name: The Lebanon Cedar of Villa Van Gilse
trees.age_estimate: roughly 120 years, from a registered planting decade

location.address: Roosendaal, Burgerhoutsestraat 12 (Villa Van Gilse garden, front of the villa)

trees.access: Free. The villa garden is, in the Rijksmonument description, 'thans toegankelijk als park'; LRMB records visitable ja, public ja, owner the municipality. The villa itself is a music school, so stay in the garden. No hours published.
trees.transport: Roosendaal station is about 1.3 km north-west, roughly a 15 minute walk via Stationsstraat and Burgerhoutsestraat.
trees.story:
The national monument listing for Villa Van Gilse names the oaks, a chestnut and a red beech from the years the house was built. It does not mention the cedar on the front lawn.

The tree register does. The Bomenstichting's Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen records a Cedar of Lebanon here, 3.03 metres round at chest height and 23 metres tall, and bands its planting to the decade 1900 to 1910, which makes it roughly 116 to 126 years old. That band is the only basis for its age. We have found no planting record, so whether it belonged to the villa's first garden or arrived a few years later is something nobody has written down. If you know, tell us.

The house behind it was built in 1900 for the factory owner J. van Gilse, to a design by the architect M. Vergouwen, and it is a Rijksmonument today. Since 1975 it has been a music school, and the garden around it is open as a park.

The register last recorded the cedar in August 2023, and an aerial photograph from spring 2026 still shows its crown in place: the only conifer on the front lawn, blue-green while everything around it stood bare.

The same garden holds two other registered trees, a plane and a catalpa, each with its own page here. The building belongs to the music students, so see the cedar from the garden.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the only conifer on the front lawn of Villa Van Gilse, blue-green and evergreen when the trees around it are bare. It is the only cedar the register lists in this garden.

trees.name: The Himalayan Cedar of the Paterstuin
trees.age_estimate: roughly 120 years, from a registered planting decade

location.address: Roosendaal, Kade 23, Paterstuin behind the Onze Lieve Vrouwekerk

trees.access: Free. Garden of the Onze Lieve Vrouwekerk (Kade 21-23), opened to the public as a park on 2015-07-16, open in daylight, gate closes at dusk (2015 municipal report); the gemeente tourism site inroosendaal.nl lists it as a place to visit. Walk right of the church and monastery to the back. Garden stays parish property; the 2015 agreement on opening ran to 2025 and renewal is not confirmed, hence flagged.
trees.transport: Roosendaal station is about 0.5 km east, a 6 minute walk along Kade.
trees.story:
When the Paterstuin was renovated in 2014 and 2015, a beech, a lime and a weeping ash from the national tree register came down. The Himalayan cedar stayed.

It grows in the garden the Redemptorist fathers laid out behind the Onze Lieve Vrouwekerk after 1868: an ornamental garden between two arms of the Watermolenbeek, with a pond, a bridge, a crucifix and a conservatory. Only on 16 July 2015 did it open to the public as a park.

The Bomenstichting's Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen, which spells it 'Hymalaia ceder', bands the cedar's planting to the decade 1900 to 1910, so it is roughly 116 to 126 years old. That band is the only basis for its age, and nobody has recorded who planted it. It is 2.75 metres round at chest height and 18 metres tall, and the register last recorded it in March 2023.

Two honest warnings. Several evergreens stand around the pond, and an aerial photograph cannot tell them apart, so our pin is the register's point rather than a fix at the trunk: look for the cedar, not the pin. And the garden still belongs to the parish. It opens in daylight and the gate closes at dusk, under a 2015 agreement that ran to 2025; we have not confirmed it was renewed. If you find the gate locked in daytime, or the cedar gone, tell us.

A registered horse chestnut stands at the west end of the same garden.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the cedar among the evergreens around the pond, 2.75 metres round and 18 metres tall; it is the only cedar the tree register lists in the Paterstuin. Walk to the right of the church to reach the garden.

trees.name: The Horse Chestnut of the Paterstuin
trees.age_estimate: roughly 120 years, from a registered planting decade

location.address: Roosendaal, Kade 23, Paterstuin behind the Onze Lieve Vrouwekerk

trees.access: Free. Same garden and conditions as roo_017: open in daylight since 2015, gate closes at dusk, parish property, opening agreement ran to 2025 and renewal is not confirmed.
trees.transport: Roosendaal station is about 0.5 km east, a 6 minute walk along Kade.
trees.story:
Of the horse chestnuts in the row at the west end of the Paterstuin, only one still grows the way a horse chestnut wants to. The national tree register counts three trees, one in natural form and two pruned into candelabras, and records the rest of the row as dead.

The Bomenstichting's Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen bands the row's planting to the decade 1900 to 1910, so it is roughly 116 to 126 years old. It gives one girth for the whole entry, 3.49 metres round at chest height, and a height of 16 metres, without saying which trunk it measured. Read it as the row's figure, not a promise about any one tree.

By that girth, nothing on the register is now larger in this garden. An oak and a sycamore nearby were taken off the monumental list in the latest update for their modest size and condition, and a beech, a lime and a weeping ash were felled when the garden was renovated in 2014 and 2015.

The Redemptorist fathers laid the garden out after 1868, and it opened as a public park on 16 July 2015. It is still parish ground, open in daylight with the gate closing at dusk, under an agreement that ran to 2025 and that we have not confirmed was renewed. Our pin is the register's point, so look for the row rather than the pin, and tell us if you find the gate shut.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the chestnut row at the west end of the Paterstuin: one tree with a full natural crown beside two pruned into candelabras. The garden lies behind the Onze Lieve Vrouwekerk, to the right of the church.
